title: Day 1 — The Legal EA/PA Role, Communication & Managing Up

frames.title: Day 1 Agenda
frames.text:
Welcome to Day 1: The Legal EA and PA Role, Communication and Managing Up.

We'll start with the difference between EA and PA work and the legal basics every assistant needs. Then we move through communication and gatekeeping, confidentiality and boundaries, and the command hierarchy and liaison work, before finishing with managing up, client profiling and the dossier, and two frameworks for written communication.

By the end of today, you'll have a clear picture of what a Legal Executive Assistant actually does day to day, you'll know when to escalate rather than act alone, and you'll be ready to manage up with the Three C's.

frames.title: Legal EA Task Overview
frames.text:
Six areas cover most of what a Legal Executive Assistant handles day to day: calendar and scheduling, correspondence and email, document and case support, court and filing coordination, billing and client support, and confidentiality and compliance.

Each one comes with real tasks and a sample from Elias's world, like blocking two hours of prep before every deposition, or flagging a client's retainer once it drops below 25 percent. Get these right, and his court dates, deadlines and clients stay protected.

frames.title: Meet Elias Thorne — Live Q&A
frames.text:
In the live class, your trainer steps into the role of Elias Thorne for a few minutes, in character, before you open a single document about him.

Here, take a moment to think about what you'd ask him, the way you'd ask a new executive on your actual first day. How does he prefer to communicate, and how will you know if you've gotten it wrong? What's the one thing that would lose his trust fastest?

Hold on to those questions. You'll build the real dossier right after this.

frames.title: EA vs. PA Roles
frames.text: Section 1 of 8: EA versus PA Roles. We'll look at the two mindsets, how the work context differs side by side, and the decision principles behind each.

frames.title: EA vs. PA: Two Mindsets
frames.text:
Before you touch any request, you need to know which hat you're wearing.

As an EA, you're looking after the business: your boss's time, his decisions and the firm's results. As a PA, you're looking after the person: his family, his errands, the life that keeps him able to work. The trouble starts when we answer a business problem with errand energy, or treat a family matter like a board meeting.

So first, when something lands, we ask one quiet question: am I protecting the business, or the person? Next, we check the dossier. If the answer's there, we use it.

frames.title: EA vs. PA: Two Mindsets
frames.text: Then, if it's honestly unclear, we play it safe and treat it as business work until we can confirm. Handling something important like a small errand is the costlier mistake.

frames.title: EA vs. PA: Two Mindsets
frames.text:
Once we've picked, we commit. Business work gets a careful, by-the-book response; personal work gets a warm, flexible one. And finally, if we got it wrong, we say so, fix it and remember the example. That's how this instinct gets sharper.

Here's a situation. A new assistant keeps one to-do list for Elias: 'Board deck edits, dry cleaning, Meridian call notes, flowers for Sarah, expense report.' By Wednesday the dry cleaning is done and the board deck isn't. What went wrong, and how would you sort that list?

frames.title: EA vs. PA: Side-by-Side Work Context
frames.text:
Both roles earn the same trust. What changes is the setting.

Picture two calls: a firm partner about a filing, and Elias's wife about a school event. You'd sound different on each, and you should. The office runs on structure, policy and formality; the personal side runs on relationships and the person's own preferences. Read which one you're in before you respond.

First, we remember that each side has its own secrets. Office secrets are contracts, money and HR matters; personal secrets are family, health and lifestyle. Protecting one doesn't cover the other.

frames.title: EA vs. PA: Side-by-Side Work Context
frames.text:
After that, we stay inside our own role. As an EA we filter and prioritize on the executive's behalf; as a PA we handle day-to-day things directly. And finally, when the two overlap, like a personal matter with real business risk, we say so out loud.

Try this one. Elias texts late at night, 'Book the usual table for Friday, and send the Meridian team the updated timeline.' Which half is which, and how do you handle each?

frames.title: EA vs. PA Decision Principles
frames.text:
The same kind of request can deserve two different answers. Take a request to move a meeting. On the business side, we ask whether it matters to money, deadlines or legal risk, and protect it if it does. On the personal side, we start from what the person prefers.

Neither answer is wrong. What goes wrong is using the wrong set of rules without noticing.

frames.title: EA vs. PA Decision Principles
frames.text: First, we name which track we're on. Next, on the business track, important work goes first, we narrow things down before bothering the executive, and we know which calls are ours. Then, on the personal track, the person's wishes lead. We offer options instead of saying no, and we keep private matters private.

frames.title: EA vs. PA Decision Principles
frames.text:
After that, if a decision doesn't fit either set of rules, we escalate. That's not the moment to trust our gut. Finally, every so often we look back at our own calls, to catch ourselves slipping into one habit for everything.

Try this one: Elias wants to move a client call to attend his daughter's recital, but that client is mid-negotiation. Which rules apply, and what do you actually do?

frames.title: Typical Work Environment
frames.text: The job looks different depending on where you land. A corporate office, a law firm, a remote startup or a private family home: similar tasks, very different expectations. Even guessing wrong about which email system they use can slow down your whole first week. So in any new role, spend the first days learning how this place works.

frames.title: Typical Work Environment
frames.text:
First, we fit our response to the setting. When a vendor lets us down, an EA pushes back or escalates professionally; a PA just gets the problem fixed. Next, clashing meetings: an EA moves things by business priority; a PA checks what the person would prefer. Finally, when a request quietly grows beyond our job, an EA points out the contract line; a PA asks permission before going further.

Here's a situation. A catering vendor sends the wrong order to a client lunch at the office, and the same vendor is booked for the Thornes' dinner party on Saturday. How does your EA side handle the lunch, and your PA side handle Saturday?

frames.title: Legal Basics
frames.text: Section 2 of 8: Legal Basics. Who's who in a law firm, the life of a legal matter, and the legal terms you'll hear every day.

frames.title: Who's Who in a Law Firm
frames.text:
Before you can route a single request well, you need to know who's who.

Partners own the firm and the client relationships. Associates are lawyers doing much of the day-to-day legal work. Of counsel are experienced lawyers with a looser tie to the firm. Paralegals do real legal work under a lawyer's supervision, and we, the assistants, keep everyone's time, communication and logistics running. Outside the firm, there are clients, opposing counsel, court clerks, judges' chambers, court reporters and experts.

frames.title: Who's Who in a Law Firm
frames.text:
First, in week one, we get the org chart. Next, for each of Elias's matters, we write down the team: partner, associate, paralegal and client contact. Then the outside names: opposing counsel, the judge and our vendors. After that, before passing anything on, we ask who owns that decision. Legal judgment goes to a lawyer. Finally, we address people properly: 'Judge Rivera' in writing, 'Your Honor' in court.

Now a situation. A voicemail says, 'This is Mark from Harlow's side, about the deposition.' Before you call back, who is Mark, and who at the firm should handle it?

frames.title: The Life of a Legal Matter
frames.text:
If you know which stage a matter is in, you can see the next deadline coming.

Everything a firm works on is called a matter. A lawsuit starts with intake and a conflict check, then an engagement letter and a retainer. Then investigation, then pleadings, the complaint and the answer. Then discovery, where both sides exchange documents and take depositions. Then motions, settlement or trial, judgment and maybe an appeal, and finally closing the file.

Deals run a shorter path: intake, engagement, drafting and negotiating, signing, then the follow-up.

frames.title: The Life of a Legal Matter
frames.text: First, when a matter opens, we note whether it's litigation or a deal, and which stage it's in. Next, at intake, we collect every party's name and every key date. Then we calendar each deadline the moment it's triggered.

frames.title: The Life of a Legal Matter
frames.text:
After that, before any hearing, trial or signing, we build the checklist early. Finally, at closing: the final bill, any trust money returned, a closing letter and the file archived.

Here's a quick one to think about: why might a lawyer be alarmed if you said a document was 'filed' when it was only 'sent'?

frames.title: Legal Terms You'll Hear Every Day
frames.text:
One misunderstood word can send the wrong document to the wrong place.

The plaintiff brings the case and the defendant answers it; someone without a lawyer is 'pro se'. A complaint starts a lawsuit, an answer responds, a motion asks the court to do something, and a brief argues why. An affidavit is a sworn statement signed before a notary; a declaration is signed under penalty of perjury, without a notary.

In discovery, interrogatories are written questions, a deposition is sworn testimony outside court, and a subpoena orders someone to show up or hand over documents. A stipulation is something both sides agree on.

frames.title: Legal Terms You'll Hear Every Day
frames.text:
First, we keep a one-page glossary in our own words and add to it every week. Next, when we hear a term we don't know, we write it down and look it up. Then we use each document's exact name. After that, we learn the firm's own words, like matter number and retainer. Finally, we notice which side the firm is on in each matter.

Now try this. Elias leaves a voice note: 'Opposing counsel served interrogatories and noticed Harlow's CFO for deposition; calendar the responses and get a court reporter.' Translate it into a plain-English task list.

frames.title: Client Intake & Conflict Checks
frames.text:
Taking on the wrong client can force a firm off a case, so the first job with any new inquiry is the conflict check.

It's an ethics rule: the firm can't take on anyone who'd clash with a current or former client. Until the check clears and an engagement letter is signed, the caller is a prospective client, so we take only what we need and give no advice. And a date mentioned in passing at intake matters.

frames.title: Client Intake & Conflict Checks
frames.text: First, we use the intake form every time: all parties, related businesses, opposing counsel, a short description and any dates. Next, we search every name, including former names and parent companies. Then any match goes to the attorney. We don't decide whether it's a real conflict.

frames.title: Client Intake & Conflict Checks
frames.text:
After that, any deadline mentioned goes to the attorney the same day. Finally, once cleared, we prepare the engagement letter and open the matter only after it's signed.

Here's a situation. A caller wants to sue 'Northgate Logistics' over a warehouse contract that ended 'almost six years ago.' What do you search, what do you flag, and what do you not say?

frames.title: Communication & Gatekeeping
frames.text: Section 3 of 8: Communication and Gatekeeping. Why gatekeeping is not 'no', the filtering matrix, and scripts that redirect without alienating.

frames.title: Basic Communication Principles for Legal EAs
frames.text:
In legal work, a message that can be read two ways is a risk, not just a style problem.

A busy attorney wants the facts fast. A nervous client wants to understand and feel reassured. A court clerk wants it formal and by the book.

So first, before we write a word, we decide who's reading it. Next, we write it so there's only one way to understand it. Then we set the tone for that reader. After that, we remember that confidentiality covers conversations too, even a casual chat in the hallway. Finally, when we have to say 'not now', we use tried-and-tested phrases, so we sound professional instead of flustered.

Here's a situation. In the lift, a colleague from another team asks, 'Did the Meridian thing settle? I heard it was big money.' The settlement is confidential. What do you say, without sounding rude or confirming anything?

frames.title: Quick Check
frames.text:
Quick check. Updating a client on a filing you just made, should the tone be A, plain language and reassuring, focused on what it means for them? B, skipped, because clients don't need filing updates? C, as brief as possible with no context? Or D, identical to what you'd send the court clerk?

Take a second.

It's A: plain language and reassuring. Reading the audience means the same event gets a different register for the client than for the court or the attorney.

frames.title: Gatekeeping Is Not 'No'
frames.text:
Good gatekeeping never slams the door. It says 'not right now, but here's what we can do.'

A flat no makes people go around you. A calm, confident 'not now, here's a better option' keeps the relationship and still protects the executive's time. And when you speak for him, you carry his authority, so there's no need to sound apologetic.

frames.title: Gatekeeping Is Not 'No'
frames.text: First, we never make the person feel wrong for asking, or tell them they should have planned better. That wins us nothing.

frames.title: Gatekeeping Is Not 'No'
frames.text:
After that, we always hand them something real: a specific time, a named colleague or a clear timeline. Finally, if they push back, we listen, explain the real constraint honestly and appeal to what we both want, instead of repeating the same no louder.

Here's a situation. A junior partner has asked for time with Elias three times this week and is getting frustrated. Elias can't meet until next week. How does the partner leave feeling heard, with a real next step?

frames.title: The Filtering Matrix
frames.text:
Not every request deserves the same speed. Answer them in the order they arrived, and the important one gets buried under five easy ones.

Instead, we run each request through four questions, in order. Does it affect money? Does it carry legal risk? Does it need the executive himself? Is there a relationship on the line? If any single answer is high, it's urgent. One serious reason is enough.

frames.title: The Filtering Matrix
frames.text: Then, if everything scores low, we decide whether to hand it to someone else, schedule it for later or offer another option.

frames.title: The Filtering Matrix
frames.text:
After that, we jot down how we sorted it, especially anything we parked, so our thinking can be checked later. Finally, we come back to parked items exactly when we said we would. A forgotten item is as bad as a mishandled one.

Now think about this. Elias's oldest client asks, 'Can he sign a birthday card for our CEO today?' It scores low on money, legal risk and authority. Why might it still go near the top of the list?

frames.title: Scripts That Redirect Without Alienating
frames.text:
Having a few ready-made ways to redirect people means we never have to improvise a clumsy no.

If the request is fine, just badly timed, we defer it. If it belongs to someone else, we re-route it. And if there's simply no room, we say so plainly and offer something else. We call that one Drastic Contrast.

First, when we defer, we give a real timeline, not a vague 'soon'. Then, when we re-route, we name the right person and make sure the handoff actually happens.

frames.title: Scripts That Redirect Without Alienating
frames.text:
After that, when we're being plainly honest, we tell the truth about the constraint and immediately offer a specific alternative. Finally, whichever we use, we try to get a small yes first, like confirming what they need.

Now a situation. You re-routed a client's billing question to finance a week ago. Today the client emails Elias directly, annoyed that nobody replied. What went wrong with your redirect, and what do you do now?

frames.title: Phone & Voicemail Etiquette
frames.text:
For a lot of clients, your voice on the phone is their first impression of the whole firm.

A good message lets the attorney act without calling us back: who called, from where, their number, which matter, what they need, how urgent it is and when to reach them. And we don't confirm that someone is a client until we know who we're talking to.

frames.title: Phone & Voicemail Etiquette
frames.text: First, answer with the firm's name and your name. Next, take the full message, read the number back, and ask which matter and whether there's a deadline. Then transfer warmly: tell the attorney who it is and why before connecting.

frames.title: Phone & Voicemail Etiquette
frames.text:
After that, when you leave a voicemail, say your number slowly at the start and the end, keep it short and leave out anything confidential. Finally, log important calls and return them within one business day.

Here's a situation. A caller says, 'I'm a reporter. Is Harlow Industries one of your clients? I just need a yes or no.' What exactly do you say, and what do you do after the call?

frames.title: Executive Presence in Action
frames.text:
Whether you're speaking as an EA or a PA, the instinct is the same: protect first, sort it out second.

Say someone calls asking for confidential information. As an EA, we're firm, brief and procedural: we can't release that, and we'll escalate it internally. As a PA, we're warm but just as protective: that's private, but we're happy to help with logistics. Both keep the door closed. One protects the business, the other the person.

frames.title: Executive Presence in Action
frames.text:
First, when something sensitive comes in, we decide in that moment whether we're answering as an EA or a PA. Then, when someone keeps pushing, we hold the same line. The EA asks for it in writing; the PA takes a message and promises a follow-up.

Here's a situation. A caller from a national newspaper asks whether Thorne and Partners is representing a well-known CEO in a fraud case. Two minutes later, Sarah Thorne's friend calls asking whether Elias and Sarah are 'going through a rough patch.' Answer the first as an EA and the second as a PA.

frames.title: Quick Check
frames.text:
Quick check. In the 'Persistent Caller' scenario, does the EA's scripted response focus on A, immediately connecting the call? B, promising a callback within the hour? C, asking for a written request to review priority? Or D, ignoring the caller entirely?

Take a second.

It's C: asking for a written request to review priority. It filters the request into a reviewable, prioritized channel, rather than granting or flatly denying access.

frames.title: Virtual Meetings & Transcription Accuracy
frames.text:
The record of a meeting can't depend on technology alone. When the recording fails, or everyone remembers a different decision, the assistant is the one people ask what was agreed. So the record is our job, not the software's.

First, we test the recording before the meeting starts. Halfway through is too late. Next, we always have a person taking notes as a backup. Then, we capture what was decided and who's doing what, and leave out the side chatter and off-the-record comments.

frames.title: Virtual Meetings & Transcription Accuracy
frames.text:
After that, if an AI tool made a transcript, we read it and clean it up before anyone else sees it. Finally, we give the executive what he actually needs: a short briefing memo, not forty pages of transcript.

Here's a situation. The AI transcript of a client call spells the client's company wrong, records a side comment about opposing counsel and lists an action item nobody agreed to. What do you fix before anything is shared, and what goes to Elias?

frames.title: Confidentiality & Boundaries
frames.text: Section 4 of 8: Confidentiality and Boundaries. Professional standards, authorization protocols, and what an assistant can and can't do.

frames.title: Professional Standards & Confidentiality
frames.text:
Everything we see is protected, but business secrets and personal privacy work a little differently.

On the business side, we're guarding contracts, financial numbers and ideas the firm owns, with real laws and HR rules behind them, so we know those rules ahead of time. On the personal side, we're guarding a family's privacy, and what holds that together is trust more than rules, so discretion is the default.

Either way, if we're not sure whether something is confidential, it is.

frames.title: Professional Standards & Confidentiality
frames.text:
We treat every channel as risky. A chat in the lift can do as much damage as a misdirected email. And when in doubt, we protect it. Over-protecting costs almost nothing; a leak can cost everything.

Here's one to think about. In the lobby, a friendly paralegal from another firm says, 'Is Elias on the Meridian matter? I heard it's getting messy.' What do you say, and what do you avoid saying?

frames.title: Boundaries & Authorization Protocols
frames.text:
Knowing exactly how far our authority goes is what lets us act quickly without getting into trouble.

Every assistant has limits on money, access and commitments. Some are written down; many are just assumed, and the assumed ones cause problems. For example: an invoice under 500 dollars, we can approve; over that, we escalate first, every time.

So first, we check anything involving money, access or a commitment against our written limits, not our memory. Next, if it's within our limit, we handle it and note that we did.

frames.title: Boundaries & Authorization Protocols
frames.text: Then, if it's over our limit, we escalate before we act. 'It'll probably be approved' isn't approval.

frames.title: Boundaries & Authorization Protocols
frames.text:
After that, we keep business and personal systems completely separate: different calendars, storage and devices. Finally, when something's unclear, we ask: is it within policy, is it legal, and would the executive trust us doing it? If any answer is no or unsure, we escalate.

Here's a situation. Sarah Thorne asks you to book a family flight upgrade that goes 300 dollars over the travel budget Elias set. She says, 'He won't mind.' What do you do, and how do you say it to her?

frames.title: What an Assistant Can and Can't Do (Unauthorized Practice of Law)
frames.text:
Clients will ask you for legal advice, kindly and often, and saying yes even once can put the firm at risk.

Only a licensed lawyer can give legal advice, set fees, take on a case, sign court papers or appear in court. Doing that without a license is the unauthorized practice of law, and it's illegal. And because the lawyer supervises us, our slip becomes the firm's problem. The line is interpretation: telling someone what the law means for them, or what they should do, is advice.

frames.title: What an Assistant Can and Can't Do (Unauthorized Practice of Law)
frames.text: First, what we can do: schedule, gather documents, share public facts like a court's hours, and relay the attorney's advice word for word. Next, what we can't do: say whether someone has a case, what a document means for them or which option to choose. Then, when asked, we use a bridge line: 'That's a great question for Elias. I'll make sure he gets it today.'

frames.title: What an Assistant Can and Can't Do (Unauthorized Practice of Law)
frames.text:
After that, we quote the attorney exactly, or have them put it in writing. Finally, when in doubt, we treat it as advice and route it.

Then try this. A client calls: 'The other side offered $40,000. Elias is in trial all week. Just between us, should I take it?' Write exactly what you'd say.

frames.title: NDAs & Non-Disclosure Discipline
frames.text:
A non-disclosure agreement is a real legal promise, so we need to know what's in it before we rely on it.

The mistake is treating 'they signed an NDA' as a magic shield. Some have expired. Some only cover certain kinds of information. And sometimes nobody actually signed one at all.

So first, before sharing anything sensitive with a vendor, contractor or temp, we check there's an NDA on file for that exact person or company. Next, we check what it covers and whether it's still in date. Then, if we can't confirm it covers this request, we pause and verify. We don't go ahead on 'it's probably fine'.

frames.title: NDAs & Non-Disclosure Discipline
frames.text:
After that, we keep a simple list of who's signed, what it covers and when it ends, so this check takes two minutes, not an afternoon. Finally, if someone we haven't cleared asks for sensitive information, that's a flag to check, not a request to fulfil.

Here's a situation. A long-time vendor asks for the Meridian board contact list to send 'a courtesy update.' Their NDA covers IT services only. What do you tell them, and what do you check?

frames.title: Command Hierarchy & Liaison
frames.text: Section 5 of 8: Command Hierarchy and Liaison. How the command hierarchy works across different tracks, and what it takes to serve as a liaison and point of contact.

frames.title: Command Hierarchy
frames.text:
When something looks wrong, we don't fix it quietly on our own. Say a document went out without the right review. Ignoring it and fixing it ourselves are both risky.

First, we notice. We catch the issue while it's still small. Next, we assess. How big is it, how urgent, and who else does it touch? Then, we escalate, to the right person through the proper channel, not around them. Finally, we inform. The executive should hear it from us before he hears it from anyone else.

Here's a situation. At 4:30 p.m., you learn that a filing deadline for a Harlow matter document was missed at noon. Elias is in a meeting with the managing partner until 5:30. How do you make sure he hears it from you, and what do you say?

frames.title: Command Hierarchy Across Different Tracks
frames.text:
Who we report a problem to depends on which world it lives in: the office, the law firm or the household. Each has its own ladder. In a company: the CEO, the senior EA, the EA, the admin assistant. In a law firm: the managing partner, the senior legal assistant, the legal EA, the paralegal. At home: the head of the family, the estate manager, the PA, the household staff.

So first, we work out which world we're in. Next, in a company, we go up the business ladder, starting with our own executive.

frames.title: Command Hierarchy Across Different Tracks
frames.text: Then, in a law firm, we follow the stricter legal ladder, because an unauthorized decision there can become a legal problem.

frames.title: Command Hierarchy Across Different Tracks
frames.text:
After that, at home, we go through the family's own ladder. Finally, if a problem sits in two worlds at once, like a household matter with legal risk, we raise it in both.

Here's a situation. The Thornes' nanny says a man came to the door asking questions about Elias's work and took photos of the house. It's a household matter, but it might involve a case. Who do you tell, in which order, and through which chains?

frames.title: Serving as Liaison & Point of Contact
frames.text:
Gatekeeping decides who reaches the executive. Being a liaison is about connecting people who need each other.

A client needs something from Elias, a vendor needs something from staff, and it all flows through us. That only works if what comes out the other end is exactly what went in, and if people know we're the one to call.

frames.title: Serving as Liaison & Point of Contact
frames.text: First, we make sure we really understand what each side needs. Next, we carry the message accurately both ways, in words that make sense to the person receiving it. Then, we make it clear we're the one point of contact for this matter, so nobody's guessing who to ask.

frames.title: Serving as Liaison & Point of Contact
frames.text:
After that, we keep in mind which job we're doing at each moment: filtering access, or connecting two people. Finally, after the handoff, we check back with both sides to make sure it landed as intended.

Here's a situation. You passed a vendor's question to Elias on Monday, and he answered on Tuesday. On Friday, the vendor calls asking why they never heard back. What part of the liaison loop was missed, and how do you fix it?

frames.title: The Liaison Skill in Practice
frames.text:
A good liaison carries the message exactly as it was sent, in both directions, and does it quickly.

Passing a request up, it's tempting to soften it or add our own spin. Passing his answer back, it's tempting to dress up a short reply so it sounds friendlier. Both change the message. And a liaison so careful that everything slows down has failed just as much as one who lets everything straight through.

So first, we quietly work out which world the request belongs to, office, legal or household, before we route it. That's often the real job.

frames.title: The Liaison Skill in Practice
frames.text:
After that, we watch our own speed, because a slow liaison becomes a bottleneck. Finally, if we're not sure the message landed the way it was meant, we check back.

Here's a situation. A partner sends Elias a long, polite email asking him to co-author a conference paper. Elias's reply to you is: 'Not this year. Too much on.' Write the message you'd send back, accurate but professional.

frames.title: Managing Up Basics
frames.text: Section 6 of 8: Managing Up Basics. Bulletproof basics, the Three C's of managing up, and why credibility is earned, not claimed.

frames.title: Bulletproof Basics
frames.text:
Three everyday basics decide whether an executive trusts us: the inbox, the travel backup plan and the full life of a meeting.

None of this is glamorous, and that's the point. An executive judges us on whether the ordinary things always go right. A cancelled flight should be an inconvenience, not a crisis. And meetings don't end when everyone leaves the room.

frames.title: Bulletproof Basics
frames.text:
First, as each email arrives, we decide straight away: action, information only, or someone else's. Next, where it makes sense, we draft the reply in the executive's voice, so all he has to do is press send. Then, when we book travel, we line up the backup too. If the 2 p.m. flight is cancelled, the 4 p.m. is already on hold. After that, we set the agenda before the meeting; that's how we go from taking notes to shaping the result. Finally, we follow every action item through until it's actually done.

Pick the basic you're weakest on today. What's one real habit, not an intention, that would fix it this week?

frames.title: The Three C's of Managing Up
frames.text:
Every update we send gets judged on three things: is it clear, is it consistent, and can he rely on it?

Clarity means he never has to guess what we're telling him or what we need. Consistency means we do things the same way every time, so he knows what to expect. And credibility means that when we say something, it's true. That one matters most.

frames.title: The Three C's of Managing Up
frames.text: So first, before sending an update, we check it's clear. Next, we check it's consistent: our usual approach, not something improvised because today's busy. Then, if speed and reliability pull against each other, reliability wins. A quick answer that's wrong is worse than a slightly slower one that's right.

frames.title: The Three C's of Managing Up
frames.text:
After that, when we're under pressure and clarity starts slipping, we slow down and restate the main point before we hit send. Finally, every so often we reread our own recent messages, because these habits fade quietly when we're busy.

Try this one. Elias asks, 'Is the Meridian binder at the courthouse?' You think the courier picked it up, but you haven't confirmed. What's the reply that protects your credibility?

frames.title: Credibility Is Earned, Not Claimed
frames.text: We can't announce that we're credible. The executive gives us credibility, one reliable week at a time, and it comes from a few things done over and over.

frames.title: Credibility Is Earned, Not Claimed
frames.text:
First, reliability: accurate, finished and on time, every time. Next, the no-surprises rule. If we know about something, he knows about it too, even if it seems minor. Then, we treat small decisions as if they might matter, because some quietly carry money, legal or reputation risk. After that, discretion is our default, especially around investors, legal matters, family and deals. Finally, if we ever damage that trust, we rebuild it steadily. One good week doesn't undo a bad one.

Here's a situation. Last month you sent a partner the wrong version of a contract, and now Elias double-checks everything you send. What does rebuilding his trust look like over the next few weeks?

frames.title: Quick Check
frames.text:
Quick check. Does the 'No-Surprises Rule' mean A, surprises are fine as long as they're positive? B, only bad news needs to be flagged early? C, an executive should never be blindsided by something their assistant already knew? Or D, executives enjoy occasional surprises?

Take a second.

It's C. Anything the assistant already knows that could affect the executive needs to reach them proactively, good or bad.

frames.title: Client Profiling & the Dossier
frames.text: Section 7 of 8: Client Profiling and the Dossier. Building a client profile, creating a comprehensive dossier, and setting up the trackers that put it to work.

frames.title: Client Profiling
frames.text:
A client profile is something we build once, so we never have to ask the same question twice. Being asked, for the third time, whether you like morning or afternoon meetings wears down trust fast.

First, the basics: role, organization and how far their authority reaches. Next, how they like to communicate. Blunt or detailed? Written or spoken? Then, their meeting rules, like breaks between meetings and off-limits times, because those are the rules new people break most. After that, travel preferences, in enough detail to book without asking. Finally, any quirks, in plain, respectful language.

Here's a situation. A new colleague books Elias an early-morning red-eye before a court day, with three back-to-back meetings after it. Which parts of his profile would have stopped both mistakes?

frames.title: Creating a Comprehensive Client Dossier
frames.text:
A dossier goes deeper than a profile. If the profile is a quick reference card, the dossier is the full handbook, in four parts: the professional picture, the personal details that actually help, his standing instructions, and his quirks.

The test is simple: could someone who has never met Elias run his account from it?

frames.title: Creating a Comprehensive Client Dossier
frames.text:
First, the firm and his role, so the reader understands the professional setting. Next, family and personal details, but only what genuinely helps us support him. Then, his standing instructions, as clear rules anyone could follow without interpreting. After that, his quirks, in plain words, never judgment. Finally, we run that test before we call it done.

Here's a situation. A substitute books Elias a window seat in row 22 for a London flight, because the dossier said 'prefers comfortable seats.' Rewrite that entry so it can't be misread.

frames.title: Dossier Excerpt — Elias Thorne
frames.text:
Every fact in a dossier needs its reason attached, because a rule without a reason is the one that gets broken.

Take Elias's fifteen-minute debrief after key sessions. Listed on its own, it can look optional. Explain that he needs that time to process a court session before his next call, and nobody will touch it.

So first, we put each fact under the right heading: firm and role, family, standing instructions or quirks. Then, we ask what would go wrong if someone got this entry wrong. That tells us how carefully to word it.

frames.title: Dossier Excerpt — Elias Thorne
frames.text:
After that, we write for someone who's never met him, with no inside shorthand. Finally, we compare our entries with the Elias examples to make sure ours are just as specific.

Here's a situation. Elias sends his 5:30 a.m. voice notes and expects an agenda by 8. A dossier entry says only: 'Voice notes early.' What would a new assistant get wrong, and what should the entry say?

frames.title: Setting Up Client Trackers
frames.text:
The dossier is the reference book. Trackers are the everyday tools that put it into practice, updated as things happen.

We start with just three: travel, inbox and meeting rhythms. Three we'll actually keep up beat ten we'll let go stale.

First, the travel tracker holds the details that change a booking: seat, connections and whether we rebook without asking.

frames.title: Setting Up Client Trackers
frames.text: Next, the inbox tracker records the exact format he expects, like one-line summaries with the details attached.

frames.title: Setting Up Client Trackers
frames.text:
Then, the meetings tracker holds hard rules, such as no back-to-back sessions and the breaks he needs. Finally, we update every tracker the moment we learn something new.

Here's a test. Elias's London flight is delayed three hours. His travel tracker says aisle seat near the front, no connections, and rebook without being asked. What do you do before he even notices?

frames.title: Why One Client, All Ten Days
frames.text:
We use the same client for all ten days on purpose, because in a real job, what you learn keeps building.

Most training brings a brand-new person for every exercise. Real life isn't like that. You work for the same executive for months. So what we learn about Elias today will come back in the calendar work, the inbox work and the travel planning later on.

frames.title: Why One Client, All Ten Days
frames.text: First, we treat every fact about Elias as something we'll need again. Next, when a later exercise leans on something from before, we try to remember it before looking it up. That recall is part of the training. Then, if something seems to contradict what we know about him, we raise it with the trainer instead of quietly working around it.

frames.title: Why One Client, All Ten Days
frames.text:
After that, we let the repetition help us; it's what makes things stick. Finally, by the last day, we should be able to describe his rules, family and communication style from memory.

Here's a situation. On Day 3, a travel scenario says Elias prefers window seats. Your Day 1 dossier says aisle seats only. What do you do, and why does it matter to raise it?

frames.title: Written Communication Frameworks
frames.text: Section 8 of 8: Written Communication Frameworks. The ACT email framework, and BLUF, bottom line up front, in emails, updates and voice notes.

frames.title: The ACT Email Framework
frames.text:
When an executive sends a messy request, a clear reply turns it into something you can both act on.

Elias thinks fast and talks in fragments. A 5:30 a.m. voice note might have three tasks tangled together. Reply 'Got it!', and we find out three days later that we misunderstood. ACT fixes that.

First, we acknowledge: we restate the request in our own words, so any misunderstanding shows up right away. Next, we clarify: we ask only what we can't work out ourselves, and we check the dossier first.

frames.title: The ACT Email Framework
frames.text: Then, we give a timeline: what will happen, by when and who owns it.

frames.title: The ACT Email Framework
frames.text:
After that, we keep it short, answer first. Finally, we send it quickly, right after the request arrives, not as a summary hours later.

Try drafting one. Elias's voice note says: 'Move the Meridian call, get me something on the Singapore thing, and find out why the retainer invoice hasn't gone out.' What's your ACT reply?

frames.title: BLUF: Bottom Line Up Front
frames.text:
If Elias reads only your first line, he should already know what you need and by when.

BLUF stands for Bottom Line Up Front. The decision, the answer or the action goes in the very first sentence; everything after it is detail he can stop reading at any time. It feels backwards, because most of us were taught to explain first. But busy people often only read the first line.

First, before we write, we finish this sentence: 'The one thing Elias needs to know or decide is...'. That becomes our first line. Next, we label the ask: 'Decision needed', 'FYI, no action', or 'Approval by 3 p.m.'.

frames.title: BLUF: Bottom Line Up Front
frames.text: Then, we add only the details he needs to act: dates, amounts, names and options, in a few short lines.

frames.title: BLUF: Bottom Line Up Front
frames.text:
After that, we move the background below a clear break or into an attachment. Finally, we finish with the exact next step and deadline, then reread just the first line the way he would.

Here's a situation. An update to Elias begins: 'Hi Elias, hope your trip was good! So yesterday I spoke to the courier, then the clerk…' The question he needs to answer is in the fourth paragraph. Rewrite just the first line.

frames.title: BLUF in Practice: Emails, Updates & Voice Notes
frames.text:
Bottom line first works everywhere: emails, chat messages, status updates, voice notes and phone calls. On a call, it sounds like 'Quick one: I need a yes or no on the retainer.' On a phone screen, the first eighty characters should tell the whole story.

First, the subject or first line carries the bottom line, with a label like Decision, FYI, Action Taken or At Risk. Next, one line on why it matters today, usually the deadline or the consequence.

frames.title: BLUF in Practice: Emails, Updates & Voice Notes
frames.text: Then, we give only the details needed to act, in short points.

frames.title: BLUF in Practice: Emails, Updates & Voice Notes
frames.text:
After that, we close with the next step and who owns it, and attach the background instead of pasting it in. Finally, we check the preview: would the first line alone make sense on a phone?

One last situation. It's 2 p.m., and a filing due at 5 p.m. is at risk because the courier is delayed; your backup is e-filing. Write the subject line and first line of the status update to Elias.

frames.title: Practice Lab
frames.text: Now it's your turn. In the Client Dossier and Gatekeeping Practice, you'll build a comprehensive client dossier and preference trackers for Elias Thorne, respond to a real ACT-framework voice note, then practice inbound gatekeeping under pressure.
